transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-05
Start time (UTC): 16:30
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Park (CTO - Ironwood), Mark Rivera (Infra Lead), Sasha Kim (Head of MLOps)

Summary:
Ironwood is evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private for latency-sensitive clinical inference. Primary drivers: data governance (PHI), VPC/on-prem path, predictable reserved GPU capacity with the ability to burst for marketing spikes, and strong audit/KMS requirements. They want a hands-on benchmark and a clear pricing+SLA picture before committing.

Topics covered:
- reserved node sizing and burst allowances
- isolation/topology (tenant fencing, warm pools, pre-warm)
- VPC peering, on-prem option and KMS/HSM integration
- benchmark plan (models, sequence lengths, latencies)
- compliance docs and next steps

Action items (also in metadata): Jordan to send pricing and compliance docs; Priya to prepare benchmark plan; Ironwood to share traffic histograms and SLOs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. I'm Jordan from Redwood, account executive, and with me I've got Priya who will handle the technical side. How are you all?
[00:06] Elena: Hi Jordan, good thanks. I think we'll be about 45ish minutes; we've got a couple of items, namely data governance and burst capacity.
[00:12] Jordan: Perfect, that's what we want to cover. Priya, quick intro?
[00:15] Priya: Hi all, Priya Singh, solutions engineer. I'll walk through topology options and then we'll dive into what a benchmark run would look like.
[00:22] Mark: Mark here, infra. We're mainly concerned about VPC peering, egress, and making sure PHI never leaves our control.
[00:27] Sasha: Sasha, MLOps. I want to understand pre-warm, cache behavior, and how burst is handled — plus the SLA for tail latency.
[00:34] Jordan: Great. High level: Redwood provides Hosted (API), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC or on-prem). For Ironwood's PHI constraints we're typically seeing Dedicated or Private. Is that the right framing?
[00:44] Elena: Yes. We want isolation plus the ability to have predictable cost — but also the ability to handle bursts from, say, a campaign or a batch rerun.
[00:51] Jordan: Understood. Priya, do you want to run through Dedicated topology options?
[00:54] Priya: Sure. For Dedicated we can offer reserved node pools — you pick the number of GPU nodes (e.g., 4 A100/80GB equiv), and we keep them warm for you. There's a warm-pool / hot-pool concept so short bursts (seconds to minutes) can be handled without cold starts. We also support burst tokens — so if you exceed the reserved pool we can spill to a shared burst tier or pre-allocated burst nodes depending on the contract.
[01:20] Priya: Important nuance: the warm-pool reduces latency but costs more; you can size based on 99th percentile tail-latency and your QPS distribution. We ask for a histogram of traffic (1m/5m/1h) to recommend sizing.
[01:34] Mark: Quick Q: those burst nodes — do they run in our VPC or do they go to a shared Redwood backend? We have strict egress rules.
[01:40] Priya: Good question. There are two models. For Dedicated (hosted) burst to shared capacity, that traffic routes through Redwood's managed infra — so data-in-flight is TLS encrypted and we have contract provisions for ephemeral logs. For Private/VPC deployments we can configure a private burst path where burst nodes run in a customer-dedicated VPC or in your on-prem cluster via the private control plane so data never leaves your network. There's an additional setup and usually a higher base commitment.
[02:06] Elena: So, if we want zero egress, we'd need the Private on-prem or VPC-hosted burst nodes, correct?
[02:11] Priya: Correct. VPC peering or customer-managed nodes ensure traffic stays within your cloud. On-prem is possible if you want air-gapped inference.
[02:18] Sasha: What's the typical RTO for burst capacity? If we blow past reserved for, say, a sudden 2k QPS peak for 10 minutes, how quickly can Redwood pre-warm extra nodes?
[02:26] Priya: It depends: warm-pool pre-warm keeps N nodes instantly available; for autoscale to additional nodes we typically see cold-starts in the 30s-90s range unless you use a template to pre-warm the model weights — that gets it down to a few seconds for kernel readiness. We also support a hot-pool prewarm for ephemeral spikes which brings up nodes in under 20s in many cases. We should size the hot-pool to your expected short-window peak to avoid the cold start entirely.
[02:49] Mark: And what about the KV cache? Our models rely heavily on KV cache reuse across requests — will that be preserved across pre-warmed nodes?
[02:58] Priya: The KV cache is per-model instance. With continuous batching and session affinity we can pin a user's session to a warmed instance to maximize cache hits. For a burst to new nodes, cache miss rates will go up until the nodes build the cache. We can mitigate by seeding common prefixes or using a shared prefix cache — depends on your workload. We'll put that in the benchmark plan.
[03:18] Elena: Security — we need to ensure encryption at rest and KMS support. Also, audit logs with 1 year retention for compliance.
[03:25] Jordan: We support customer-managed KMS for key wrapping; HSM integrations are available for Private deployments. Our hosted Dedicated offers KMS + default audit logs; for sensitive customers we route the control plane to customer VPC and offer longer retention as an add-on. I'll send SOC 2 and ISO docs after the call.
[03:40] Sasha: Is SSO/SAML and RBAC available for per-team controls? 
[03:44] Priya: Yes we integrate with SAML/SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and role-based access controls that map down to cluster namespaces.
[03:51] Mark: Any constraints around model size? We're planning to run one 70B dense model and a 12B quantized model at 96k context for specific workflows.
[03:59] Priya: Long context models are supported but influence kernel selection and memory. For 96k contexts you need adequate GPU memory — we typically suggest model quantization and using attention optimizations. For a 70B with 96k you may want model sharding or multi-GPU inference; that affects latency. We'll capture that precisely in the benchmark.
[04:18] Elena: We're trying to avoid time-of-day throttles for clinicians. The 99th percentile tail must be under 300ms for short queries (<=512 tokens). Is that realistic?
[04:27] Priya: With warm nodes and affinity caching, sub-300ms for short sequences is achievable on A100-class or better when the model fits on a single GPU and batching is tuned. For long context or sharded models, tail latency rises. We'll model both scenarios.
[04:40] Jordan: Quick callout: cost vs latency tradeoff. Keeping a large warm-pool drives predictable latency but increases monthly committed spend; burst tokens reduce commitments but can increase tail latency in edge cases.
[04:52] Sasha: That cost tradeoff is the big decision for us. We need to justify reserved spend to finance.
[04:57] Mark: Also, what happens during infra failures? If a reserved node is preempted, do you have automatic fallback to hosted models?
[05:04] Priya: Yes, Redwood supports smart routing and automatic fallback policies. You can configure fallback to a lower-cost compatible model or to hosted multi-tenant capacity. For Dedicated with SLA we provide reserved failover pools and rapid node replacement. We'll share the SLA specifics in the docs.
[05:18] Elena: On the Private path, how much involvement is required from our side to get an on-prem package running?
[05:24] Priya: For on-prem there's an install bundle and a managed control-plane agent. We need network and storage access, and an initial engineering integration, typically a 2-3 week lift for a pilot, depending on your environment. For VPC-hosted Private, it's usually faster — a few days to configure peering and IAM.
[05:40] Mark: Any limits on the number of simultaneous sessions? We have batch jobs and interactive clinician sessions — very different profiles.
[05:47] Priya: We treat them separately; the routing layer can direct batch to specific GPU pools with longer latency tolerance while interactive goes to low-latency reserved nodes. Rate limits can be per-route and token-level.
[05:59] Sasha: Let's talk benchmarks — what do you need from us to make the run meaningful?
[06:03] Priya: We'll need model artifacts (or container), a small representative dataset, traffic shape (histograms), desired SLOs (p50/p95/p99), and any session stickiness rules. For KV-cache heavy workflows, we'll add synthetic prefixes to exercise cache hit/miss cases.
[06:19] Elena: We can provide models and a sanitized dataset — some PHI, though, so we'll sandbox the bench. We prefer the test either in VPC or on-prem for that reason.
[06:28] Priya: That's fine. For the bench we'll propose two runs: one in Dedicated hosted with VPC peering and a second in a Private VPC/on-prem configuration to validate zero-egress.
[06:38] Jordan: And we'll include cost delta estimates for each.
[06:41] Mark: About pricing — do you charge for burst token usage per-second or per-token?
[06:45] Jordan: Burst is typically billed per-second for node time plus per-token compute cost where applicable. We can provide a worked example based on your traffic. For commitments, we offer a blended monthly rate for reserved nodes.
[06:56] Sasha: Any prior clients in healthcare doing PHI-heavy workloads on Dedicated?
[07:00] Jordan: Yes, we have a handful; we can anonymize references and case studies. We'll also share our standard BAA and security pack.
[07:08] Elena: Good. One regulatory item — audit logs need to be immutable and we might need 7-year retention for certain workflows. Is that possible?
[07:15] Priya: Standard retention is 1 year but for enterprise Private deployments we can enable longer retention and S3 Glacier-like tiers. It will be part of the contract add-on. We'll note that.
[07:25] Mark: Let's talk numbers — for a pilot we're thinking 4 reserved nodes, ability to spike to 12 nodes for up to 20 minutes twice a day. How would that look?
[07:34] Priya: That pattern suggests a warm-pool of 4 and a hot-pool of 8 for bursts. If the bursts are predictable (twice a day) we can pre-schedule weighted pre-warm windows to reduce cold-starts. Pricing will include the committed base cost plus an hourly rate for hot-pool usage.
[07:50] Jordan: We'll give you two pricing options: one with a cold-start tolerant burst (lower commit) and one with a hot-pool (higher commit, lower latency).
[07:58] Sasha: For the prewarm, do you support setting which models are resident in which node pools? We have a small and a large model, and we want the small to live in the interactive pool.
[08:06] Priya: Yes you can tag model routes and pin them to specific pools. We'll include recommended labels in the runbook.
[08:12] Elena: On telemetry — we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency dashboards.
[08:18] Priya: Redwood Console has per-route dashboards, token cost, trace IDs and sampling. For Private we can mirror telemetry into your observability stacks and forward traces.
[08:28] Mark: A nit: what's your expected lead time to get dedicated reserved nodes active after contract?
[08:32] Jordan: Typically 2-4 weeks for hosted Dedicated depending on capacity availability. For Private/VPC it's closer to 1-2 weeks for VPC-hosted and 2-3 weeks for on-prem pilot. Exact times in the SLA.
[08:46] Sasha: For the bench run, could we also test an A/B: quantized model vs dense, to understand cost/latency tradeoffs?
[08:53] Priya: Absolutely. We'll include a quantization run and measure latency, memory, and token throughput.
[08:59] Mark: Any redwood-internal terms we should know — like preemption, eviction policies?
[09:04] Priya: For dedicated reserved there's no preemption for your reserved pool. For burst to shared infra, there may be preemption under extreme conditions, but we provide automated fallback routing. We'll capture eviction windows and RTOs in the doc.
[09:16] Elena: Let's surface potential blockers now. For us: 1) must have KMS integration and private peering; 2) cost justification for reserved spend; 3) must pass bench with p99 < 300ms for short queries. Anything you need from our side right away?
[09:31] Jordan: Please share the traffic histograms and the sanitized dataset. We'll follow up with the compliance pack and a pricing sheet. Priya will send the benchmark plan.
[09:41] Sasha: One more question — can Redwood restrict logs ingested by the service? We don't want token strings stored unencrypted in logs.
[09:48] Priya: By default we redact user content from standard logs for Dedicated customers; for Private deployments you can set strict log scrubbing and have logs forwarded only to your storage. We'll include the exact log-scoping options.
[09:59] Mark: Great. If the bench looks good, what's the procurement timeline? We want to close pilot approval fast.
[10:04] Jordan: Many customers do a 30-day pilot then convert to a 6-12 month commit. We'll provide a pilot agreement template for legal review.
[10:11] Elena: Ok. Can we get the security docs and pricing by early next week?
[10:15] Jordan: Yes, expect docs by Thursday (2026-01-08).
[10:18] Priya: I'll draft the benchmark plan by Friday and propose times for the run.
[10:22] Sasha: We'll prepare the sanitized data and traffic histograms this week.
[10:26] Jordan: Perfect. Any other questions?
[10:29] (brief pause)
[10:33] Elena: Not right now. Thanks, this was helpful.
[10:36] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the security pack and a proposed schedule.
[10:41] Mark: Thanks.
[10:43] Sasha: Thanks, bye.
[10:44] Jordan: Bye.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: Automatic transcription, medium confidence; some product names occasionally mis-transcribed (e.g., hot-pool as hotpool or Redwood Private transcribed as Redwood Privat). Some timestamps approximate speaker changes.
